difficultyReason: Two-concept gap: stimulus links 'board-certified' to 'eligible for hospital privileges' and separately asserts a physician is board-certified; conclusion is about hospital privileges. Student must supply the missing universal conditional. One reversed-conditional trap and one 'tends to' weakener are included.
stimulus: Only board-certified physicians are eligible for hospital privileges at Renfield Medical Center. Dr. Okafor has recently completed the board certification process and been formally certified. Therefore, Dr. Okafor is eligible for hospital privileges at Renfield Medical Center.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All physicians who are eligible for hospital privileges at Renfield Medical Center are board-certified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any physician who completes the board certification process is thereby board-certified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Okafor has applied for hospital privileges at Renfield Medical Center.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most physicians who are board-certified eventually receive hospital privileges at some institution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renfield Medical Center grants hospital privileges to all physicians who meet its credentialing standards.

explanations.correct: The stimulus tells us only board-certified physicians are eligible (i.e., eligible → board-certified) and that Dr. Okafor completed the process and was 'formally certified.' The one gap is whether completing and being 'formally certified' entails actual board certification. Choice B closes that gap universally: anyone who completes the process is board-certified. With B added, the chain is: Dr. Okafor completed the process → board-certified (B) → eligible for privileges (stimulus premise). The conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus already states only board-certified physicians are eligible (eligible → board-certified). Choice A restates that same direction (eligible → board-certified) and adds nothing new; it does not establish that board-certified physicians ARE eligible.
explanations.C: Whether Dr. Okafor has applied is irrelevant; the conclusion concerns eligibility, not whether an application has been submitted. This introduces an extraneous step not in the argument.
explanations.D: 'Most' is too weak — sufficient-assumption answers must close the gap to certainty, not probability. This does not force the conclusion about Dr. Okafor specifically at Renfield.
explanations.E: This shifts the subject to 'credentialing standards,' a different concept from board certification. It does not establish that board-certified physicians satisfy those credentialing standards.

difficultyReason: Two-step conditional chain in an economics context. Stimulus establishes that price controls cause shortages and that shortages reduce consumer welfare; conclusion is that a proposed rent-control ordinance will reduce consumer welfare. Student must link rent control to price controls. One too-weak trap and one partial-bridge trap present.
stimulus: Price controls on any commodity inevitably cause shortages of that commodity. Whenever shortages of a commodity arise, consumer welfare is reduced. The city council is considering a rent-control ordinance that would cap monthly rents on all residential units. Consumer advocates who support this ordinance are therefore mistaken in believing it will benefit consumers.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rent-control ordinances are a form of price control on residential housing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any ordinance that reduces consumer welfare will ultimately harm the local economy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Price controls on commodities other than housing tend to cause more severe shortages than rent controls do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Consumer welfare can be reduced even when rents are lower than they would otherwise be.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever consumer welfare is reduced, price controls are the cause.

explanations.correct: The chain in the stimulus runs: price controls → shortages → reduced consumer welfare. The conclusion says the rent-control ordinance will reduce consumer welfare. The gap is that rent control has not been identified as a price control. Choice A supplies exactly that link: rent-control ordinances ARE price controls. With A added, the full chain fires, and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.B: This extends the conclusion further (to harm the local economy) rather than closing the gap between rent control and the stated conclusion about consumer welfare. Irrelevant extension.
explanations.C: Comparative severity of shortages is irrelevant; the argument needs any shortage to trigger reduced welfare, not a comparison of magnitudes. Also uses 'tend to,' which is too weak.
explanations.D: This is a partial-bridge trap. It asserts that welfare can be reduced even under lower rents, but it does not establish that rent control is a price control or that this ordinance will in fact reduce welfare — it only says such reduction is possible.
explanations.E: Reversed-direction trap. The stimulus flows from price controls to reduced welfare; Choice E asserts that every case of reduced welfare is caused by price controls. This is the converse and is neither needed nor sufficient for this argument.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy domain. Stimulus establishes that any action violating individual autonomy is impermissible, then concludes a mandatory organ-donation default policy is impermissible. Gap: student must link the policy to a violation of autonomy. Reversed-conditional and subject-shift traps present.
stimulus: Any policy that violates individual autonomy is ethically impermissible. Critics of the proposed default organ-donation policy argue that it removes an individual's right to refuse donation unless that individual takes active steps to opt out. These critics are correct that the policy is ethically impermissible.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any policy that requires individuals to take active steps to exercise a right violates individual autonomy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Organ-donation policies should always reflect the express wishes of the individual.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Policies that are ethically impermissible are never enacted into law in a just society.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Individual autonomy is violated only when a person is physically prevented from taking action.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most default policies in liberal democracies are designed to promote the common good rather than individual rights.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: (1) autonomy violation → ethically impermissible; (2) the default policy requires active opt-out steps. The conclusion is that the policy is ethically impermissible. The gap is that requiring active opt-out steps has not been connected to violating autonomy. Choice A closes that gap universally: any policy requiring active steps to exercise a right violates autonomy. With A, the chain is complete and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.B: This is a principle that sounds relevant but uses different vocabulary ('express wishes') and does not logically force the conclusion that the policy is impermissible. Too vague to close the gap.
explanations.C: This extends the argument beyond its conclusion (to whether the policy becomes law) and does not connect the policy to being impermissible in the first place. Irrelevant extension.
explanations.D: This actually undermines the argument by narrowing the definition of autonomy violation to only physical prevention, which would make it harder — not easier — to conclude the policy violates autonomy.
explanations.E: 'Most' is too weak and introduces a comparative claim about liberal democracies that has no bearing on whether this specific policy is ethically impermissible.

difficultyReason: Environmental science domain. Two-concept gap: stimulus links habitat fragmentation to species extinction risk and then invokes a specific logging plan; conclusion is about extinction risk. Reversed-conditional and too-weak traps present.
stimulus: Every large-scale logging operation that fragments old-growth forest habitat significantly increases the extinction risk of species dependent on that habitat. The Kessler Timber Company's proposed logging plan will fragment over 400 square kilometers of old-growth forest in the Cascade Range. Conservationists are therefore justified in claiming that the plan will significantly increase extinction risk for species dependent on Cascade old-growth habitat.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Species dependent on old-growth habitat in the Cascade Range are already classified as threatened under federal law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Kessler Timber Company's plan constitutes a large-scale logging operation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fragmentation of old-growth habitat significantly increases extinction risk only when the fragmented area exceeds 500 square kilometers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any operation that significantly increases extinction risk for native species will fragment old-growth forest habitat.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most logging operations in the Cascade Range have historically caused some degree of habitat fragmentation.

explanations.correct: The stimulus's universal claim applies to 'every large-scale logging operation.' The conclusion applies this to the Kessler plan. The gap is that the Kessler plan has not been established as large-scale. Choice B supplies exactly this: the plan IS a large-scale logging operation. With B, the modus ponens fires: large-scale operation that fragments old-growth → increased extinction risk; Kessler's plan is a large-scale operation (B) that fragments old-growth (stimulus) → conclusion follows.
explanations.A: Existing threatened status is irrelevant to whether the plan increases extinction risk. This is an extraneous fact that does not close the logical gap.
explanations.C: This actually undermines the argument by setting a 500 km² threshold, whereas the plan only fragments 400 km². Adding this assumption would prevent the conclusion from following.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus says large-scale fragmentation → increased extinction risk. Choice D reverses this: increased extinction risk → fragmentation. The reversed form does not license the conclusion.
explanations.E: 'Most' is too weak, and historical patterns about other operations do not establish anything about the Kessler plan specifically.

difficultyReason: Law/legal reasoning domain. Two-concept gap between 'hearsay evidence' and 'inadmissibility' and a claim about a specific statement. Reversed-conditional and partial-bridge traps present.
stimulus: Any out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter it asserts is hearsay evidence. No hearsay evidence is admissible in a trial proceeding unless it falls within a recognized exception. The defense attorney argues that the witness's account of what the bystander told her should be excluded from trial. The defense attorney's argument is sound.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The witness's account of what the bystander told her is an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter it asserts, and it falls within no recognized hearsay exception.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No out-of-court statement is ever admissible in a trial proceeding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bystander's statement was unreliable because the bystander had poor visibility at the time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any evidence that is inadmissible in a trial proceeding should be excluded by the defense attorney.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hearsay evidence is inadmissible in a trial proceeding only when it is prejudicial to the defendant.

explanations.correct: The argument needs two things established about the witness's account: (1) that it IS hearsay (out-of-court statement offered to prove truth) and (2) that no exception applies. The stimulus's general rules handle the rest. Choice A provides both elements in a single universally applicable bridge. With A, the chain is: out-of-court + offered to prove truth = hearsay (premise 1); hearsay + no exception = inadmissible (premise 2); inadmissible = should be excluded (implicit in legal practice). The conclusion that the defense attorney's argument is sound follows necessarily.
explanations.B: Too broad — the stimulus itself carves out recognized exceptions for hearsay, and premise one only addresses statements offered for truth. This overgeneralization contradicts the stimulus's structure.
explanations.C: Reliability concerns about the bystander's vision are a different basis for exclusion (credibility) unrelated to the hearsay rule invoked in the stimulus. Subject-shift trap.
explanations.D: This reverses the relevant role: it is the judge, not the defense attorney, who excludes evidence; more importantly, it does not establish that this particular evidence is inadmissible in the first place.
explanations.E: This introduces a new condition (prejudice to the defendant) not mentioned in the stimulus's hearsay framework, and it narrows admissibility in a direction that doesn't close the gap about this specific statement.

difficultyReason: Technology/computer science domain. Two-concept gap: stimulus links 'open-source code' to 'publicly auditable' and 'publicly auditable' to 'more secure'; conclusion is about a specific system. Reversed-conditional and too-weak traps.
stimulus: Any software system whose source code is publicly auditable is more secure against undisclosed vulnerabilities than a system whose code is proprietary. The city's new traffic-management system relies entirely on open-source components, every line of whose code is available for public inspection. City officials who worry that the system is less secure than a comparable proprietary system are therefore mistaken.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any software system composed entirely of open-source components has source code that is publicly auditable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Software systems used by municipal governments are more frequently targeted by malicious actors than privately operated systems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A software system is more secure against undisclosed vulnerabilities only if its developers actively respond to publicly reported flaws.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most open-source software projects receive more external security audits than proprietary systems of comparable complexity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any system that is more secure against undisclosed vulnerabilities relies on open-source components.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states: publicly auditable → more secure (premise 1). The traffic-management system uses open-source components with all code available for public inspection. The conclusion says the system IS more secure. The gap is that 'open-source with code available for public inspection' has not been formally equated to 'publicly auditable.' Choice A closes this: any system composed entirely of open-source components IS publicly auditable. With A, the chain is: open-source system (A) → publicly auditable → more secure (premise 1). The conclusion follows.
explanations.B: The frequency of attacks on municipal systems is irrelevant to whether this system is more or less secure than a comparable proprietary one. This is an extraneous comparative claim.
explanations.C: This introduces an additional necessary condition (active developer response) that would actually undermine the conclusion rather than support it, since the stimulus's conditional does not include this caveat.
explanations.D: 'Most' is too weak — sufficient-assumption answers must force certainty. Even if most open-source projects get more audits, this does not guarantee this system is more secure.
explanations.E: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus says publicly auditable → more secure; this choice reverses to more secure → open-source. This does not license the inference that the open-source system is more secure.

difficultyReason: Linguistics domain. Two-concept gap: stimulus links 'language with no native speakers' to 'extinct language' and concludes about a specific language (Dalmatian). Reversed-conditional, subject-shift, and too-weak traps present.
stimulus: A language that has no remaining native speakers is, by the standard definition used in comparative linguistics, an extinct language. Scholars of Romance languages have documented that Dalmatian, a language once spoken along the eastern Adriatic coast, has had no native speakers since the death of its last known fluent speaker in 1898. It follows that Dalmatian is an extinct language.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dalmatian is classified within the Romance language family by comparative linguists.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No language that has ever had native speakers can be fully reconstructed from written records alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The standard definition used in comparative linguistics applies to Dalmatian.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any language classified as extinct by comparative linguists had no native speakers for at least a century before being so classified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most languages that lose their native speakers are eventually replaced by a dominant regional language.

explanations.correct: The stimulus's first premise invokes 'the standard definition used in comparative linguistics' to define extinct language. The conclusion applies this definition to Dalmatian. The gap is whether that standard definition actually applies to Dalmatian — perhaps Dalmatian is excluded from the definition's scope for some reason. Choice C closes this gap directly: the standard definition DOES apply to Dalmatian. With C, the chain is complete and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: That Dalmatian is in the Romance family is already implied by the stimulus; moreover, being a Romance language does not by itself determine whether the comparative-linguistics definition applies to it. Subject-shift trap.
explanations.B: Reconstructibility from written records is entirely irrelevant to the definition of extinction used in the argument. Extraneous concept.
explanations.D: Reversed-direction trap. This describes a condition for classification (extinct → no speakers for a century) rather than establishing that the no-speakers condition triggers extinction. It also introduces a time threshold not present in the stimulus.
explanations.E: 'Most' is too weak and speaks to language replacement, not to whether Dalmatian specifically qualifies as extinct under the stated definition.

difficultyReason: History domain. Argument concludes a Roman general's campaign was unjustified; premises establish that unjustified campaigns are those launched without senatorial authorization and that this campaign lacked such authorization. Gap: student must link the specific general's campaign to the no-authorization premise. Partial-bridge and reversed-conditional traps.
stimulus: In the late Roman Republic, any military campaign launched by a general without prior authorization from the Senate was, by Roman constitutional convention, an unjustified campaign. Julius Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon River in 49 BCE with his army was a military campaign launched without prior senatorial authorization. Historians who characterize that crossing as constitutionally justified are therefore in error.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Julius Caesar was aware that crossing the Rubicon without senatorial authorization violated Roman constitutional convention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any campaign that is constitutionally unjustified in Roman terms was launched without prior senatorial authorization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Roman constitutional convention during the late Republic was the appropriate standard by which to evaluate the justification of Caesar's crossing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No Roman general ever received retroactive senatorial authorization for a campaign already under way.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Caesar's political motivations for the crossing were self-serving rather than directed at the welfare of Rome.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: no senatorial authorization → unjustified (under Roman constitutional convention). Caesar's crossing lacked authorization (premise 2). The conclusion is that historians who call it 'constitutionally justified' are in error. The gap: one could argue Roman constitutional convention is the wrong standard, or doesn't apply. Choice C closes this: Roman constitutional convention IS the appropriate standard for evaluating Caesar's crossing. With C, the argument is airtight — the conclusion that the crossing was unjustified, and that historians calling it justified are wrong, follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Caesar's awareness of the violation is irrelevant to whether the campaign was constitutionally unjustified. The argument is about objective constitutional status, not mens rea.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus already establishes no authorization → unjustified. Choice B gives the converse: unjustified → no authorization. This does not license a new conclusion and is not what is needed.
explanations.D: Retroactive authorization is a novel concept not present in the stimulus's framework. Even if true, it does not close the gap about whether the convention applies to evaluate this crossing.
explanations.E: Caesar's motivations are irrelevant to the constitutional analysis; the argument relies solely on the authorization criterion, not intent.

difficultyReason: Policy/public health domain. Two-step conditional chain: mandatory disclosure → informed consent preserved; informed consent preserved → policy is ethically permissible. Conclusion targets a specific pharmaceutical pricing policy. Too-weak and reversed-conditional traps present.
stimulus: A pharmaceutical pricing policy is ethically permissible only if it preserves patients' informed consent regarding treatment options. Any policy that requires mandatory disclosure of all available therapeutic alternatives to patients preserves their informed consent. The federal government's proposed tiered-pricing policy for insulin includes a mandatory disclosure requirement covering all available therapeutic alternatives.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion that the proposed tiered-pricing policy is ethically permissible to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Preserving patients' informed consent is sufficient for a pharmaceutical pricing policy to be ethically permissible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proposed tiered-pricing policy will make insulin more affordable for most patients who currently cannot access it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any pharmaceutical pricing policy that is ethically permissible includes a mandatory disclosure requirement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Informed consent is preserved in most cases where patients receive some information about treatment alternatives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Federal pharmaceutical policies are subject to ethical review only when they affect a broad population of patients.

explanations.correct: The stimulus gives: (1) ethically permissible → preserves informed consent (necessary condition only); (2) mandatory disclosure → preserves informed consent; (3) the policy has mandatory disclosure. From (2) and (3), the policy preserves informed consent. But (1) only says preserving informed consent is necessary, not sufficient for permissibility. The conclusion requires it to also be sufficient. Choice A supplies exactly this: preserving informed consent IS sufficient for permissibility. With A, the chain closes: policy has disclosure (3) → preserves informed consent (2) → ethically permissible (A).
explanations.B: Affordability is an entirely separate ethical consideration not invoked in the stimulus's framework. This is an extraneous concept that does not close the logical gap.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus's premise says mandatory disclosure → preserves informed consent, and the question is about sufficiency for permissibility. Choice C asserts permissible → mandatory disclosure, the converse of what the argument needs.
explanations.D: 'Most cases' and 'some information' are both too weak; sufficient-assumption answers require universal force. This does not guarantee that this policy preserves informed consent.
explanations.E: The scope of ethical review applicability is irrelevant to whether this policy, once subject to ethical evaluation, is permissible.

difficultyReason: Arts/aesthetics domain. Stimulus concludes a critic's negative review of a minimalist sculpture is unfounded; gap requires linking 'deliberately evoking discomfort' to 'aesthetic merit.' Reversed-conditional, subject-shift, and too-weak traps present.
stimulus: Art critics sometimes dismiss works that deliberately evoke discomfort in the viewer as lacking aesthetic merit. This dismissal is unfounded whenever the discomfort is integral to the work's intended meaning. The sculptor Nadia Voss has stated that the visceral unease her installation 'Threshold' provokes is not incidental but is the precise vehicle through which the work communicates its meaning. The critic who recently dismissed 'Threshold' as lacking aesthetic merit was therefore unjustified.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any work in which deliberately evoked discomfort is integral to the work's intended meaning possesses aesthetic merit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Art critics who dismiss works as lacking aesthetic merit rarely engage with the artist's stated intentions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A critic is unjustified in dismissing a work as lacking aesthetic merit only when the work has received acclaim from other critics.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Works that possess aesthetic merit are those that deliberately evoke discomfort in the viewer.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The aesthetic merit of an installation is usually best assessed by examining the artist's own account of the work's purpose.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: dismissal is unfounded when discomfort is integral to intended meaning (premise 1); Voss says the discomfort in 'Threshold' IS the vehicle of its meaning, i.e., integral to intended meaning (premise 2). The conclusion is that the critic's dismissal was unjustified. The gap: 'unfounded dismissal' needs to be connected to 'unjustified' dismissal. More precisely, we need that when discomfort is integral to meaning, the work HAS aesthetic merit — so that dismissing it as lacking merit is factually wrong, and therefore unjustified. Choice A closes this: any work where integral discomfort is present possesses aesthetic merit. With A, 'Threshold' has aesthetic merit, so the critic's claim that it lacks merit is wrong, making the dismissal unjustified.
explanations.B: Whether critics generally engage with artist statements is a sociological observation irrelevant to whether this dismissal was unjustified. Extraneous.
explanations.C: This introduces an external criterion (acclaim from other critics) not present in the stimulus's reasoning, and as a necessary condition for unjustified dismissal it would actually make the conclusion harder to draw.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus's framework implies integral-discomfort → aesthetic merit; Choice D asserts aesthetic merit → deliberately evokes discomfort. This is the converse and does not force the conclusion.
explanations.E: 'Usually' is too weak to force the conclusion. Moreover, this speaks to assessment method rather than to whether 'Threshold' in fact possesses aesthetic merit.
